key_insight: This review shows that control theory, optimal transport, probabilistic inference, thermodynamics, and machine learning are deeply connected through a shared mathematical structure. By translating ideas across these fields, it reveals a unified way to understand and design learning algorithms.
problem_solved: AI research often develops powerful methods in separate subfields with different terminology, making it hard to see how they relate or when one framework can inform another. This paper addresses the challenge of connecting these parallel perspectives into one coherent conceptual map.
method: Synthesizes core principles from five areas: control theory, optimal transport, probabilistic inference, non-equilibrium thermodynamics, and learning.
Explains how these fields describe similar optimization, dynamics, and transport processes using different mathematical languages.
Connects theory to applications to help readers transfer intuitions and tools across disciplines.
impact: For AI/ML practitioners, this provides a unified framework for thinking about optimization, generative modeling, inference, and dynamics. It can help researchers choose better algorithms, interpret existing methods more clearly, and discover new cross-disciplinary approaches.
visual_elements: A central hub-and-spoke diagram showing the five fields connected through shared mathematical ideas.
A flow diagram illustrating how data, probability distributions, and control objectives transform across frameworks.
Side-by-side comparison panels mapping equivalent concepts across each discipline.
An application pipeline showing theory flowing into learning algorithms and real-world use cases.
paper_title: Bridging Control, Inference, Transport, and Thermodynamics: From Theory to Applications in Learning
paper_authors: Emmy Blumenthal, Nikolas Claussen, Benjamin Eysenbach, Catherine Ji, Gautam Reddy
